The two most popular intermediate splits, side by side

PPL vs Upper/Lower: Which Split Should You Choose?

Short answer: Choose upper/lower if you train four days a week or want a simpler schedule. Choose push/pull/legs if you can train five or six days and like shorter, more focused sessions. At their best-fit schedules, both train most muscles about twice a week.

Push Pull Legs vs Upper/Lower in brief

Push pull legs and upper/lower are the two splits most intermediate lifters end up choosing between. Both group muscles so that you are not training the same ones on consecutive days, and both can produce excellent results when volume and effort are sensible.

The real difference is the number of days each one asks of you. Upper/lower is built around four sessions; PPL is built around six. Everything else — session length, recovery demands and flexibility — follows from that.

Ideal lifterIntermediate or advanced, happy to train 5–6 daysBeginner to advanced, training 4 days

Key differences explained

Training frequency and weekly volume

On six days, PPL gives each muscle two sessions and plenty of room for volume, because each session only covers one third of the body. Upper/lower reaches the same twice-a-week frequency in four days, but each session covers a lot more muscles, so you usually do fewer sets per muscle per session.

Session structure

A push day groups chest, shoulders and triceps; a pull day groups back and biceps. That keeps sessions focused, but the muscles in a day overlap (for example pressing fatigues the triceps before you reach them). Upper days mix pushing and pulling, which helps spread fatigue, though the sessions can run long if you pack too many exercises in.

Recovery

Upper/lower leaves two full rest days a week and gives each half of the body at least a couple of days before it is trained again. PPL on six days leaves only one rest day, so sleep, food and stress matter more, and a lighter week now and then is usually necessary.

Flexibility

If life interrupts a four-day upper/lower week, you can shift sessions and still hit everything. Miss a push day on a six-day PPL and chest, shoulders and triceps lose a weekly session, so PPL rewards a predictable schedule.

FAQ

Can I run PPL on four days?

You can run push, pull, legs and then an upper or lower day, but most muscles are trained once or twice depending on how you arrange it. If four days is your limit, upper/lower is usually the cleaner choice.

Is upper/lower better for strength?

Often, yes, because it lets you practise the main lifts twice a week while leaving more recovery than a six-day schedule. Full body is the other strong strength option on fewer days.

Which is better for muscle gain?

Neither is better by default. Muscle gain responds to total weekly sets, effort and consistency, so the split you can sustain at the right volume is the better one.
